h1: 10 Best Things to Do in Phrae
intro: Phrae is a small town in the shadow of northern Thailand's mountains that has kept its old-world character intact — a sacred hilltop temple, pastel-colored former royal residences, indigo-dyed mo hom fabric you won't find anywhere else, and garden cafes made for slowing down. Here are the 10 attractions real visitors talk about most, with entry fees, locations and trip-planning tips. Spend a day wandering the old town on foot or drive up to the Rong Kwang viewpoints for an overnight stay — either way works.

blocks.html:
Phrae's charm is that it's an old town that's easy to explore on foot yet packed with things to see. The highlights cluster inside the old city walls, in the inner-town district known as Nai Wiang — walk a few steps and you'll come across century-old teak houses, the pastel gingerbread-style Khum Chao Luang mansion, the pink Vongburi House with its intricately carved fretwork, and old temples tucked down the lanes. On Saturday evenings, Kham Lue Road turns into Kad Kong Kao, a cultural walking street where you can graze on local northern food and shop for mo hom indigo fabric at the same time. Just outside town there's Phra That Cho Hae on a hill to the east, Phae Mueang Phi with its earth pillars and clay walls carved into strange shapes by wind and rain, and Ban Thung Hong, the original home of Phrae's indigo cloth. Nature lovers and cafe hoppers can also drive up to Rong Kwang to sleep above a sea of mist along the "sky road." It all connects easily — whether you're into temples and blessings, old towns, crafts, or cafes.

This list includes the pins you shouldn't miss in Phrae, like Wat Phra That Cho Hae, the royal temple and birth-year stupa for those born in the Year of the Tiger, whose octagonal chedi clad in gilded copper sheets gleams in the sun — a beloved temple that merit-seekers make a point of visiting. There's Khum Chao Luang, now the Phrae city museum and once a filming location for the TV drama Roy Mai; Vongburi House, a 120-plus-year-old pink teak wedding house covered in gingerbread carvings by Cantonese craftsmen; Wat Chom Sawan, Phrae's only Burmese Bagan-style temple built entirely of teak; and Ban Thung Hong, the home of mo hom fabric where you can try a tie-dye workshop yourself. Cafe lovers get Kae Dam Tham Suan, a vintage garden cafe in town, and Nomad Cafe & Bar, a cafe by day and bar by night in the Kad Kong Kao quarter. Scroll on for the details of each spot and plan your own route.

blocks.name: Wat Phra That Cho Hae (Royal Temple)
blocks.signature: The birth-year stupa for those born in the Year of the Tiger — an octagonal Chiang Saen-style chedi clad in gleaming gilded copper, set on a low hill. Phrae's most revered temple and a must for merit-makers
blocks.descHtml:
If you only have time for one stop in Phrae, locals will point you straight to "Wat Phra That Cho Hae," the royal temple that has stood with the people of Phrae for centuries. It sits on a low hill about 9 kilometers east of town — an easy drive of under twenty minutes. This is the birth-year stupa for people born in the Year of the Tiger, so merit-seekers come in a steady stream, though anyone born in any year is welcome to pray for blessings.

The unmissable highlight is the Phra That Cho Hae chedi itself, a 33-meter octagonal stupa in the Chiang Saen–Lanna style, clad entirely in gilded copper sheets (thong changko) that glow golden in the sun — many say it looks like a smaller Phra That Doi Suthep. Sacred Buddha relics are enshrined inside. Within the temple grounds you'll also find Phra Chao Than Jai, Phra Buddha Lokanat, and an old teak viharn to pay respects at and explore.

As for the atmosphere, most reviews agree that weekdays are quiet and uncrowded, while weekends and the annual Phra That Cho Hae worship festival (around March) get very busy. The climb to the stupa is a naga staircase of a hundred-plus steps; if that's too much, there's an elevator for a 20 baht fee. Entry to the temple is free, with a large parking lot, restrooms, and plenty of souvenir and food stalls.

A few things to know: this is a genuinely sacred temple where people come to worship, so dress modestly, and mornings offer the best light and cooler air. The temple is open daily from roughly 06:00 to 19:00. Its Google rating of 4.7 from thousands of reviewers confirms it as one of Phrae's top destinations.
mustOrder: The Phra That Cho Hae chedi — a 33-meter octagonal stupa clad in gilded copper
Pay respects at the Year of the Tiger birth-year stupa
Phra Chao Than Jai and the old teak viharn
Climb the naga staircase / take the elevator for hill views
blocks.bestFor: Merit-seekers visiting their birth-year stupa + the first stop of any Phrae trip

blocks.name: Phae Mueang Phi (Phae Mueang Phi Forest Park)
blocks.signature: Otherworldly earth pillars and clay walls sculpted by millions of years of wind and water erosion, with the Pha Pho Lae viewpoint and an easy nature trail — photogenic from every angle
blocks.descHtml:
Phae Mueang Phi — officially "Phae Mueang Phi Forest Park" — is a place where nature spent millions of years slowly eroding soil and sandstone into earth pillars, clay walls and strange rock columns. Some look like mushrooms, some like pagodas, some like fairy-tale castles. If you enjoy unusual natural landscapes, easy walks and great photos, this is the spot — it's Phrae's most famous natural landmark, and locals are proud to say no visit to Phrae is complete without it.

The must-do here is following the nature trail into the main cluster of earth pillars standing in rows like a stone forest, then continuing up to the "Pha Pho Lae" viewpoint higher up, where you look down over the pale-brown pillars set against the surrounding green forest — an angle many visitors say is beautiful from every direction. Plenty of real reviews agree the park isn't huge; 30 minutes to an hour covers it, making it better as a stop along the way than a full-day destination. There's also a famous grilled-chicken restaurant at the entrance worth a bite.

Check the entry fee and opening hours before you go, as sources don't fully agree — sometimes entry is free, sometimes there's a maintenance fee of around 20 baht per person plus a vehicle fee. Hours are roughly 08:30–16:30 daily. It's located in Nam Cham subdistrict, Mueang Phrae, about 15 km northeast of town — an easy drive of under half an hour, with a large parking lot.

Good to know: the sun here is strong and shade is scarce, and some stretches of the trail are sandy. Go in the early morning or late afternoon to avoid the midday heat, wear comfortable walking shoes, and bring water and a hat. If it has just rained the path can be a little slippery, so watch your step — and you'll head home with a full set of gorgeous earth-pillar photos.
mustOrder: Walk among the earth pillars and clay walls
Pha Pho Lae viewpoint
The nature study trail
Grilled chicken at the park entrance
blocks.bestFor: Fans of unusual landscapes + photography — visit early morning or late afternoon

blocks.name: Khum Chao Luang (Phrae City Museum)
blocks.area: Khum Doem Road, Nai Wiang, Mueang Phrae, Phrae
blocks.signature: A Thai-European gingerbread-style mansion built in the early reign of King Rama V, once a filming location for the drama Roy Mai — the lord's chambers upstairs, an underground jail below, free to visit
blocks.descHtml:
If you're exploring Phrae's old town with time for only one stop, many people will send you to "Khum Chao Luang" first. This was the residence of Chao Piriyathepwong, the last ruling lord of Phrae, built around 1892 (early in the reign of King Rama V). It's a two-story brick-and-stucco mansion in the "gingerbread" style — the Thai-European hybrid architecture fashionable at the time. The details everyone photographs are the fretwork carvings along the eaves and gables, and the doors and windows said to number 72 in all. It's a natural fit for history lovers, architecture fans, and anyone who enjoys a leisurely old-town stroll.

There are highlights on every floor, literally. Upstairs you'll find the lord's chambers, antique household items, and reception rooms that keep their original atmosphere. What people talk about most, though, is the space beneath the house, which was once used to imprison convicts and slaves. One review on Wongnai puts it plainly: "it's good, but maybe a little spooky" — there are small square openings once used to look in on prisoners, and illustrations of the punishments of that era. The mansion's other claim to fame is that it was a main filming location for Channel 3's drama "Roy Mai" — if you've seen the series, standing in front of the house will feel instantly familiar.

Budget-wise it couldn't be easier: it now operates as the Phrae city museum with free admission, open daily 08:30–16:30. The location is right in the heart of the walled old town on Khum Doem Road in Nai Wiang, near Naree Rat School — you can walk or cycle on to Vongburi House and the old temples in the neighborhood in a single outing.

Good to know: the building is a registered historic monument, so tread gently and don't touch the exhibits. Most of the information signs are in Thai — if you want the deeper stories, don't hesitate to ask the staff. And because it's an old wooden building, late morning to afternoon light is best for photos.
mustOrder: Gingerbread fretwork carvings + 72 doors and windows
The lord's chambers upstairs
The jail beneath the house (slave holding cells)
Filming location of the drama Roy Mai
blocks.bestFor: History and architecture lovers — half a day in Phrae's old town

blocks.name: Vongburi House
blocks.signature: A 120-plus-year-old two-story pink teak wedding house in Thai-European style, its gingerbread carvings by Cantonese craftsmen, still holding the original belongings of Phrae's noble family
blocks.descHtml:
Vongburi House — known locally as "Khum Vongburi" — is a two-story pink golden-teak wedding house in the middle of the old town that no visit to Phrae should skip. Completed around 1900, making it over 120 years old, it was a wedding gift built by Mae Chao Bua Tha, consort of Chao Luang Piriyathepwong, the last ruling lord of Phrae, for a bridal couple in the family. What stops people in their tracks is the sweet pink of the entire house set against the impossibly fine fretwork known as "gingerbread" carving, executed by Cantonese master craftsmen working alongside local artisans — a rare Lanna-Thai-meets-European style. It's perfect for history buffs, architecture fans, and photographers after that classic shot.

The must-do is heading upstairs, where the house still keeps nearly all the belongings of Phrae's noble family — old teak furniture, silverware, porcelain, vintage photographs, and rare old documents including slave purchase contracts and papers from the teak concession era. Descendants of the family still live here and run the museum themselves, so the atmosphere feels like visiting an elder relative's home rather than a stiff, formal museum.

Admission is very easy on the wallet: around 30 baht for adults, less for children, open daily roughly 09:00–17:00. The location is superb — on Kham Lue Road in Nai Wiang, a few minutes' walk from Kad Kong Kao (the Saturday walking street) and within the same radius as Khum Chao Luang and several old temples, so you can plan a full old-town walk from here.

Most real reviews praise how beautifully the house has been preserved — it even won an outstanding architectural conservation award from the Association of Siamese Architects — and say it's well worth the pocket-change entry fee. A few things to know: it's an old wooden house, so step lightly on the wooden floors, some spots prohibit photos or require removing your shoes, and it's a genuinely lived-in home — good manners keep the atmosphere pleasant for both guests and hosts.
mustOrder: The 120+ year-old pink teak wedding house with gingerbread carvings
Upstairs rooms holding the noble family's original belongings
Antique documents, silverware and original teak furniture
Photo spot in front of the pink Thai-European facade
blocks.bestFor: History, architecture and old-town photography fans — pairs well with Kad Kong Kao

blocks.name: Kad Kong Kao (Phrae Walking Street)
blocks.area: Kham Lue Road, old town, Nai Wiang, Mueang Phrae, Phrae
blocks.signature: A cultural walking street held every Saturday evening — graze on local northern food and shop for mo hom and indigo-dyed fabric among the old wooden houses of the town center
blocks.descHtml:
If your Phrae trip happens to land on a Saturday night, do not miss "Kad Kong Kao," the Phrae walking street. This cultural market takes over Kham Lue Road in the old town, near Vongburi House and Wat Pong Sunan. What sets it apart from typical walking streets is the setting: real, still-standing old wooden houses in the town center, with many vendors dressed in indigo mo hom shirts as they set up their stalls. Strolling here has that unhurried small-town feel — perfect for laid-back travelers, photographers, and families who want to wander and sample local food with the kids.

The highlight reviewers mention most is the sheer choice of local food — savory dishes, old-fashioned sweets, local fruits and vegetables, and fresh juices, all at genuinely homey market prices. The other big draw is mo hom and indigo-dyed fabric, Phrae's signature product, available as ready-to-wear clothing and community handicrafts to take home as gifts. Keep walking and you'll find little coffee shops down the sois, and a temple at the end of the street to pop into as well.

No need to worry about cost — entry is free, and a food-and-strolling budget of about a hundred baht will fill you up. It's in the old town area of Nai Wiang, Mueang Phrae, with parking easy enough to find nearby. It runs Saturday evenings only, roughly 3:30 pm to 9 pm (sometimes starting around 4 pm) — early evening is best, when all the stalls are out and the air is cooling down.

It's popular because it's both a genuine local market for Phrae people and a community project to preserve local food and crafts. Wongnai reviewers rate it positively, praising the lovely, uncrowded, easygoing atmosphere. Good to know: it only happens on Saturdays — come any other day and you'll find just a quiet old-town neighborhood — and some stalls start packing up before 9 pm, so arriving at dusk gets you the fullest selection.
mustOrder: Local Phrae food and traditional sweets
Mo hom and indigo-dyed fabric
Stroll past the old wooden houses near Vongburi House
Stop at a coffee shop down the soi
blocks.bestFor: Saturday evenings — easygoing strollers, photographers and families sampling local food

blocks.title: 🛏️ Where to stay in Phrae — the old town or a mountain-view night in Rong Kwang
blocks.text: To get the most out of Phrae, stay a night — you can wander the old town at dusk and visit Phra That Cho Hae early in the morning before the crowds. The most popular hotels cluster in the Nai Wiang district of town, within walking distance of Khum Chao Luang, Vongburi House and Kad Kong Kao, with everything from small hotels in heritage houses to boutique stays. Nature lovers who want to wake up to a sea of mist can pick a hillside homestay near Rong Kwang like Rai Lung Lon instead. Choose a location close to your first morning's sightseeing and you'll get the best value — compare prices and reviews before booking.

blocks.name: Rai Lung Lon Camping Is Life
blocks.signature: A cafe, campground and hilltop homestay with 360-degree views of rolling green Teletubby-style hills — sip coffee, barbecue, and sleep above a sea of mist on Phrae's scenic sky road
blocks.priceRange: Drinks around 100 baht · rooms from 1,300–1,500 baht/night incl. breakfast
blocks.descHtml:
Rai Lung Lon Camping Is Life is a small cafe, campground and homestay perched on a ridge along the "sky road" — Route 1343 (Phrae–Nan) — behind Wat Phra That Pu Jae in Rong Kwang district. It's ideal for campers and cafe lovers who want to escape the noise and relax among the rounded green hills locals affectionately call the "Teletubby hills." The real selling point is the wide-open 360-degree mountain view: coffee by day, barbecue in the evening, and waking up to a sea of mist in the morning, all in one place.

The must-do is settling into the camp-style cafe zone up top with a drink and letting your eyes wander along the ridgelines. If you want to stay over, there are around 7 small wooden cabins lined along the hillside, each with a balcony facing the view — on a lucky morning you open the door straight onto a sea of mist. Another favorite photo spot is the curve of the sky road near the farm, which is especially beautiful in the late-afternoon light.

Prices are friendly: drinks run about a hundred baht, and many reviews agree it's "worth it for the view." Rooms start around 1,300–1,500 baht per night for two, breakfast included. The cafe opens daily roughly 08:00–18:00 (usually earlier on holidays). The farm is about 30 minutes from Phrae town, an easy drive up Route 1343.

Before you go: the accommodation runs on solar power, so high-wattage appliances like hair dryers can't be used, and pets aren't allowed. The wind up here is strong and it gets cold, especially in winter, so pack warm layers. The most popular season is late rainy season into early winter, when the odds of catching the sea of mist are highest — call ahead to check availability and the weather before setting out.
mustOrder: Coffee with a 360-degree view of the Teletubby hills
Sleep above the sea of mist on the sky road
Evening barbecue on the hillside
Photos of the sky-road curve in the golden hour
blocks.bestFor: Campers and cafe lovers who want to sleep above the mist on the sky road

blocks.name: Wat Chom Sawan (Wat Jong Nuea)
blocks.area: Yantarakit Koson Road, Thung Kwao, Mueang Phrae, Phrae
blocks.signature: Phrae's only Burmese Bagan-style temple — an all-teak building with a 9-tiered cascading roof, built by Shan traders during the reign of King Rama V
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Chom Sawan — known locally as "Wat Jong Nuea" — is the only Burmese Bagan-style temple in Phrae. Its main building is made entirely of teak, combining the ordination hall, viharn and monks' quarters under a single roof that cascades down in castle-like tiers, decorated with wood fretwork and colored glass that catches the light. It was built through the faith of the Tai Yai (Shan) people who came to trade teak in Phrae during the reign of King Rama V. If you love old temples with a character distinct from the usual Lanna style, this is a pin you shouldn't skip.

Almost everything unmissable is inside. The highlight is "Luang Pho San," a Buddha image woven from bamboo strips and then lacquered and gilded — extremely rare — along with an ivory manuscript carved with Burmese script, an ivory Buddha image, and lacquered, gilded pillars covered in exquisite patterns. The carved wooden ceiling inlaid with colored glass is one that many reviewers say keeps your neck craned for a long while. Outside there's a central Burmese-style chedi surrounded by smaller chedis at each point. The overall atmosphere is quiet, peaceful and shaded, never crowded — easy strolling and photography.

The location is excellent, right on Yantarakit Koson Road in the old-town area, only about 1 kilometer from the provincial hall, with ample parking. Open daily roughly 08:00–16:30, free entry (with a donation box for temple upkeep). Most real reviews praise the fine woodcarving and the tranquility; some say it's a temple "unlike anywhere else" and genuinely memorable. TripAdvisor also ranks it among the top attractions in Phrae.

Good to know: the temple was registered as a national historic monument in 1990. The wooden floors and antiquities are fairly fragile, so remove your shoes inside the building, tread gently, and dress modestly — it's still an active place of worship. While you're at it, pair it with Wat Phra Bat Ming Mueang and Khum Chao Luang along the same route.
mustOrder: Luang Pho San, the woven-bamboo Buddha image lacquered and gilded
The all-teak building with its multi-tiered cascading roof
The ivory manuscript + ivory Buddha image
Carved ceiling inlaid with colored glass + the Burmese-style chedi
blocks.bestFor: Temple and architecture fans — half a day in Phrae's old town
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Andromeda Oscar / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

blocks.name: Ban Thung Hong (Mo Hom Indigo Fabric Village)
blocks.signature: The original home of Phrae's mo hom fabric — watch the natural indigo dyeing process, try a tie-dye workshop yourself, and shop for mo hom shirts and bags, the province's signature souvenir
blocks.priceRange: Free to browse and shop · workshops from around 100 baht
blocks.descHtml:
If you want a souvenir from Phrae that's truly one of a kind, Ban Thung Hong is the pin you can't skip. This is the original home of mo hom fabric (also spelled "mor hom"), an old Tai Phuan village that has dyed cloth with the hom indigo plant for over a century, until it became the province's signature — as the local saying goes, "you can't visit Phrae without taking a mo hom shirt home." The village stretches along both sides of Yantarakit Koson Road, lined with shops to browse at your leisure. It suits souvenir shoppers, anyone curious about traditional crafts, and families who want a hands-on activity for the kids.

The highlight reviewers mention most is the quality of the mo hom shirts — well-made, inexpensive, with a deep, naturally beautiful indigo color, in both traditional local cuts and modern styles, plus trousers, skirts, bags, scarves and tablecloths. The other thing not to miss is the hand tie-dye workshop, such as at the Pa Ngiam learning center, where you pick a shirt or handkerchief, tie your own pattern, and dip it in natural indigo dye mixed with ash lye and tamarind water — then hold your breath as you unfold it to see the pattern. You'll take home a piece that exists nowhere else in the world.

Budget-wise it's easy: browsing and shopping are free, and tie-dye workshops start at around a hundred baht per person (call ahead, as some places need to prepare materials). The village is in Thung Hong subdistrict, Mueang Phrae, just north of town — about 4 kilometers out along Highway 101 — easy to reach by car or hired songthaew. Most shops open during the day, roughly 09:00–17:00.

Notes from real reviews: naturally dyed indigo can bleed a little at first, so wash it separately the first few times. Some also say the village now feels more like a shopping stop than a traditional village, but if you come to pick out the genuine article, chat with the friendly shop owners, and try dyeing cloth yourself, it's well worth it — a close-up encounter with Phrae's living craft heritage.
mustOrder: Genuine indigo-dyed mo hom shirts
Hand tie-dye workshop
Watch the natural hom indigo dyeing process
Souvenirs — mo hom bags and scarves
blocks.bestFor: Souvenir and craft lovers who want to try tie-dyeing themselves

blocks.name: Kae Dam Tham Suan (Black Sheep Cafe)
blocks.signature: A vintage-style cafe in town wrapped in trees and greenery of every kind — sip coffee at ease in a shady, garden-at-home atmosphere
blocks.descHtml:
If you're exploring Phrae's old town and want a relaxed corner for coffee, "Kae Dam Tham Suan" (Black Sheep Cafe) is the place people keep mentioning. It's a vintage-style cafe in town, wrapped in trees and greenery of every kind — walk in and it feels like sitting in a friend's backyard garden, shady and cool, with both an air-conditioned glasshouse zone and an outdoor garden zone. It suits anyone escaping the bustle for some solo downtime, a date, or a work session — there are power outlets too.

The highlight many people love is the carefully arranged cactus and succulent garden corner, a photo spot that has made the cafe a social-media favorite. The palette is warm white and brown, decorated with vintage objects and plants that give it real charm. Drinks that come up often in reviews are the iced cappuccino, the fragrant iced matcha latte, and the red velvet, with bakery items to pair with your coffee. There's also a small corner selling plants, home decor, accessories and indigo-dyed fabric to browse.

Prices are very friendly — most drinks run from a few dozen baht to just over a hundred, so a budget of about 60–120 baht per person leaves you satisfied. It's in Phrae town, in the Thung Kwao area near the old town, easy to reach with parking available, open daily during the day from roughly 08:00–16:30. Early risers can have their coffee and move on to sightseeing with perfect timing.

The cafe is popular because it combines two things people love — a leafy garden atmosphere and vintage photo corners — at approachable prices. One small thing to know: it closes fairly early (winding down by mid-afternoon), so plan for morning to early afternoon, and weekends get busy. For the prettiest, quietest corners, morning is your best bet.
mustOrder: Iced cappuccino
Iced matcha latte
Red velvet
The cactus garden photo corner
blocks.bestFor: Cafe lovers who want to unwind in a garden and take pretty photos in central Phrae

blocks.name: Nomad Cafe & Bar
blocks.signature: A stylish bar-cafe in the Kad Kong Kao quarter — a laid-back cafe by day that turns into an atmospheric bar by night, with cocktails as the headliner
blocks.descHtml:
NoMad CraftBeer & Café is a stylish bar-cafe tucked into the Kad Kong Kao quarter of Phrae's old town. If you've been strolling the walking street and want a corner to sip a cold drink and unwind, this is the answer. The main draw is a wide range of craft beer — Thai, imported and on tap — combined with warm retro decor. It's a drinking spot many Phrae locals call a fresh option for a town that used to go quiet after dark.

The highlight reviewers agree on is the rotating craft beer selection that keeps things interesting, at reasonable prices, and an atmosphere intentionally built to be more than a bar — a place to sit, talk, share stories and unwind gently with friends. The food leans toward snacks and drinking bites rather than full meals; some reviews note you can even bring in food from outside if you want specific accompaniments. The retro, 90s-tinged vibe is fun to photograph, and it suits easygoing drinkers rather than fans of booming music.

The location is in the heart of Kad Kong Kao, Phrae's famous walking street, an easy walk from the old-town sights. It opens evenings into the night, roughly 18:00 to midnight, and usually closes on Tuesdays. Budget about 200–400 baht per person. Its Google rating stands at 4.7 from over 180 reviews — a solid share of very happy visitors.

A couple of small things to know: on busy nights the counter staff can be stretched thin, so you may need to order at the bar yourself — if you're coming as a group, allow a little extra time — and check the opening days before you go since it closes Tuesdays. It's a great way to end a day in Phrae's old town with a cold beer in a quiet, comfortable corner of the city.
mustOrder: Rotating craft beers (Thai / imported / on tap)
Cold draft beer with drinking snacks
The retro corner for evening photos
blocks.bestFor: Evenings and late nights — laid-back beer sippers

Great for anyone who wants an easy trip that covers everything in a single day.

items.title: Driving or renting a car is easiest
items.text: The old-town sights are within walking distance of each other, but Phra That Cho Hae, Phae Mueang Phi and Rong Kwang lie outside town in different directions, and public transport is limited. The most convenient option is renting a car or motorbike — Grab is very scarce in Phrae, so sort out your transport before heading out of town.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: Temples, museums, food at Kad Kong Kao and most mo hom fabric shops take cash only. Keep small notes handy for entry fees, parking, street snacks and donation boxes. ATMs are easy to find in town but scarce at the attractions outside it.

items.title: Mornings and evenings are best for the old town
items.text: Midday in Phrae is hot with strong sun. Touring Khum Chao Luang and the temples is far more comfortable in the morning or late afternoon. Kad Kong Kao happens only on Saturday evenings, so if the walking street is on your list, plan your days around it.

items.title: Dress modestly at temples
items.text: Phra That Cho Hae and Wat Chom Sawan are sacred places where people genuinely come to worship. Cover shoulders and knees, remove shoes where signs indicate, and keep your voice down inside the viharn.

items.title: English is limited
items.text: Outside the major tourist spots, English signs and menus are scarce. A translation app helps, or simply pointing at pictures works fine at markets and local restaurants. Most Phrae locals are kind and patient with travelers.

items.title: Take home mo hom fabric
items.text: Indigo-dyed mo hom fabric is Phrae's signature product. Stop by Ban Thung Hong to watch the dyeing process, shop for mo hom shirts and bags, or try a tie-dye workshop yourself — a souvenir unlike anything you'll find elsewhere.

blocks.title: Planning the Perfect Phrae Trip
blocks.html:
Phrae is an easy place to travel because most of the good stuff clusters in the old town — you can walk or cycle a loop covering Khum Chao Luang, Vongburi House and Wat Chom Sawan in half a day, since they all sit close together in the Nai Wiang quarter. That leaves the afternoon for driving out to Phra That Cho Hae east of town, then swinging by Phae Mueang Phi and Ban Thung Hong, which lie outside town in different directions. If you're doing it all in one day, start at Cho Hae in the morning before the sun gets strong.

If you're here on a Saturday, don't miss Kad Kong Kao on Kham Lue Road in the evening, roughly 4 pm to 8 pm — graze on local food and shop for mo hom fabric among the old wooden houses. Park near Vongburi House and walk right in. During the day, drop into a cafe like Kae Dam Tham Suan for a lazy hour in its in-town garden, and for a laid-back evening continue to Nomad Cafe & Bar in the Kad Kong Kao quarter. If you have time to spare and want mountain views and the sea of mist, drive up to Rai Lung Lon in Rong Kwang — it's worth an overnight stay since it's farther out of town than the other stops.

blocks.text: A day trip to Phrae is fun, but staying a night in the old town lets you stroll at dusk and visit Phra That Cho Hae early before the crowds — or head up to Rong Kwang to sleep above the sea of mist. Compare Phrae hotel prices and reviews before you book.

faq.q: What are the must-see attractions in Phrae?
faq.a: The pins visitors to Phrae never skip are Wat Phra That Cho Hae, the royal temple and Year of the Tiger birth-year stupa that is the province's most revered temple; Phae Mueang Phi, where earth pillars and clay walls have been eroded into strange shapes by wind and rain; Khum Chao Luang and Vongburi House in the old town, wooden mansions in Thai-European style; Kad Kong Kao, the Saturday walking street; and Ban Thung Hong, the original home of Phrae's mo hom indigo fabric.

faq.q: What is Phrae best known for?
faq.a: Phrae's highlight is an old town that still keeps its century-old teak houses intact — Khum Chao Luang, the gingerbread-style mansion where the drama Roy Mai was filmed; Vongburi House, a pink teak wedding house over 120 years old; and Wat Chom Sawan, Phrae's only all-teak Burmese Bagan-style temple — paired with Wat Phra That Cho Hae, the hilltop Year of the Tiger stupa, and the indigo-dyed mo hom fabric of Ban Thung Hong, the province's signature product.

faq.q: Are Phrae's attractions expensive to visit?
faq.a: Most are free or cost pocket change. Wat Phra That Cho Hae is free (the elevator to the stupa for elderly/disabled visitors is 20 baht), Khum Chao Luang and Kad Kong Kao are free, Wat Chom Sawan is free with a donation box, Vongburi House charges around 30 baht for adults, Phae Mueang Phi ranges from free to about 20 baht (check on site), and Ban Thung Hong is free to browse and shop, with tie-dye workshops starting at around a hundred baht. Cafes and bars charge for whatever you order.

faq.q: How do I get to and around Phrae? Is parking convenient?
faq.a: Phrae is reachable by bus from Bangkok, by train to Den Chai with an onward transfer, or by domestic flight to Phrae Airport. Once there, driving yourself or renting a car is the most convenient option since public transport within the province is limited. The old-town sights — Khum Chao Luang, Vongburi House and Wat Chom Sawan — are close enough to walk between; park near Vongburi House and you can cover several spots on foot, including Kad Kong Kao. Phra That Cho Hae, Phae Mueang Phi and Rai Lung Lon in Rong Kwang lie outside town and each has its own parking lot.

faq.q: What are the opening hours of Phrae's attractions?
faq.a: Temples like Phra That Cho Hae and Wat Chom Sawan are open from daytime into the early evening — mornings are recommended for smaller crowds and gentler sun. Khum Chao Luang and Vongburi House keep daytime office-style hours. Kad Kong Kao runs only on Saturday evenings, roughly 16:00–20:00. Cafes like Kae Dam Tham Suan open from mid-morning to late afternoon, while Nomad Cafe & Bar stays open into the night since it turns into a bar after dark. Check each place's page before setting out, as hours can shift on holidays.
